title: Time Passes · 5
paragraphs: As she lurched (for she rolled like a ship at sea) and leered (for her eyes never fell on anything directly, but only with a sidelong glance that asked to be spared the scorn and anger of the world—she was witless, she knew it), as she clutched the banisters and hauled herself upstairs and rolled from room to room, she sang. Rubbing the glass of the long mirror and leering sideways at her swaying figure, she let a sound come from her lips—something that had perhaps been cheerful on the stage twenty years before, had been hummed and danced to, but now, coming from this toothless, bonneted caretaker, was robbed of meaning. It was like the voice of witlessness, of humor, of persistence itself, trodden down but springing up again; so that as she lurched along, dusting, wiping, she seemed to be saying how it was all one long sorrow and trouble, how it was getting up and going to bed again, and getting things out and putting them away again. It had not been easy or cozy, this world she had known for close on seventy years. She was bowed down with weariness. How long, she asked, creaking and groaning on her knees under the bed, dusting the boards, how long is it to go on? But she hobbled to her feet again, pulled herself up, and again, with her sidelong leer that slipped and turned aside even from her own face and her own sorrows, stood and gaped in the glass, smiling at nothing, and began again the old amble and hobble, taking up mats, putting down china, looking sideways in the glass—as if, after all, she had her consolations; as if some incorrigible hope really did twine itself around her dirge. There must have been visions of joy at the washtub, say, with her children (though two had been born out of wedlock and one had deserted her), or at the pub, drinking, or turning over odds and ends in her drawers. There must have been some break in the dark, some channel in the depths of obscurity through which enough light came to twist her face into a grin in the glass, and make her, turning to her work again, mumble out the old music-hall song. Meanwhile the mystics, the visionaries, walked the beach, stirred a puddle, looked at a stone, and asked themselves, “What am I?” “What is this?”—and suddenly an answer was granted them (what it was they could not say), so that they were warm in the frost and had comfort in the desert. But Mrs. McNab went on drinking and gossiping as before.
